title: A Little Mind: Giving Language Model Parameters a Face
summary: I built a small, slightly strange instrument for playing with the statistical controls behind language models. It's a design experiment in making abstract systems feel understandable.
body:
I've been experimenting with local language models lately, and something about their controls has always seemed funny to me. Temperature, Top-P, Top-K, repetition penalties: a handful of little numbers can completely change how a model behaves, but they're presented as if their meaning is self-evident.

They're not really human qualities, either. A model might seem more exploratory or more rigid when you adjust them, but there isn't a clean psychological equivalent for any of these statistical mechanisms. I wanted to design around that disconnect rather than explain it away.

So I built A Little Mind. It's a compact sampling instrument with a tiny illustrated face at its center. When you turn a dial or drag a probability control, the face reacts. Let go, and it settles right back into its vacant little blinking routine. The surrounding graphics give each parameter its own visual logic, while the numeric readouts keep the instrument useful.

The public version is an interactive React prototype. Its probability distribution and generated words are simulated, explicitly, so you can play with the concepts without needing a model running. Connecting it reliably to LM Studio and other local backends is the next engineering step, along with figuring out how to package it as a proper add-on.

I like building interfaces that make complicated systems a little less opaque. This one also gets to have a face.

body:
I just finished a small but useful upgrade to the blog publisher behind emitrice.com.

The publisher now has a post history view, so I can see previously published posts and delete old ones directly from the tool. More importantly, email updates are now optional per post.
When I publish something, I can choose whether it should also send an email to subscribers. Bigger updates can still hit the inbox, while smaller notes, experiments, and quick progress posts can stay quietly on the site.

The whole flow now connects the publisher, GitHub, Render, and Resend into one cleaner system, with clearer feedback about whether a post was published and whether an email was actually sent.
